feed.title: Combined summary - Softfork before GTA VI?

entry.title: Combined summary - Softfork before GTA VI?
entry.summary: The evolution of Bitcoin softfork development has undergone significant changes over recent years. Initial enthusiasm for covenants—a mechanism that allows contractual conditions to be attached to transactions—gradually dissipated as the community shifted its attention toward emerging topics such as ordinals, inscriptions, and divisions within core development teams, which ultimately led to a major hardfork. Parallel to this, resources were redirected towards post-quantum cryptography initiatives, despite the uncertain immediacy of quantum computing threats. This shift has fostered an impression that covenants are already part of Bitcoin’s feature set, even though they have not been formally adopted or implemented. Several protocols, including Ark and the Lightning Network, suggest readiness for covenant-dependent features and rebindable signatures, yet these remain unintegrated while broader plans for future softforks proceed. There is now a unique opportunity for renewed collaboration and consensus on implementing covenants, especially in the wake of recent hardforks. The decision between adopting solutions like TEMPLATEHASH or CTV (Covenant Transaction Verification) remains unresolved, with no definitive direction established by the community. In addition to covenants, other foundational technologies such as GSR (Generic Signed Receipts) and CCV (Cross-Chain Validation) could benefit from increased focus and prioritization. Meanwhile, discussions around BIP54 continue without clear indication of whether it will be proposed as a standalone upgrade or bundled with related changes like rebindable opcodes. These deliberations highlight the broader challenge of pacing and prioritizing softforks, given the typically long intervals between protocol upgrades. Strategic decisions about where to allocate technical and community resources will shape Bitcoin's ability to deliver timely and effective improvements. Debates around new soft-forks reveal the complex interplay between innovation, risk, and community buy-in. Features once deemed too controversial, such as OP_CAT, have seen renewed consideration following proposals like [BIP-347](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/02bebeb5ef53dc21a52d5706c6b4c17b6af6c1cc/bip-0347.mediawiki), demonstrating that persistent advocacy can reopen discussions even for divisive ideas. The journey of sidechains further exemplifies this complexity. Despite insufficient support for [BIP 300](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/02bebeb5ef53dc21a52d5706c6b4c17b6af6c1cc/bip-0300.mediawiki) due to concerns such as Miner Extractable Value, developers may still pursue alternative forms of sidechains, potentially centralized ones, to bypass existing limitations. This adaptive approach mirrors broader trends in technology: when formal processes restrict progress, creative use of current tools enables innovation, but often at the cost of increased complexity and unforeseen consequences. Just as C++ developers have historically used templates and metaprogramming to extend language capabilities beyond their original design, Bitcoin developers may similarly seek ways to push the boundaries of what is possible within the protocol—even outside official channels. The question of ossification in Bitcoin is closely linked to the control of UTXOs (unspent transaction outputs). The SegWit upgrade demonstrated that those controlling large amounts of UTXOs wield significant influence over the protocol's direction, leading to the concept of "Economic Majority Rule." In the aftermath, stakeholders seeking to maintain control began consolidating UTXOs in large custodial wallets, some of which are made available as shares in ETFs across global stock markets. This concentration of control allows custodial entities to block the introduction of covenants, which otherwise could enhance non-custodial solutions like the Lightning Network by improving scalability and usability. For many users, the biggest challenges with non-custodial Lightning involve usability and costs, obstacles that custodial services mitigate by aggregating channel management. The more scalable covenants become, the less dependent the ecosystem is on custodial intermediaries. As a result, custodial interests have strong incentives to resist covenant implementation, using diversionary tactics and discouraging all efforts to advance these features to retain protocol control. The trajectory of soft-fork development is rarely linear. During the design and review phases, previously unknown vulnerabilities can emerge, necessitating immediate attention and sometimes shifting priorities away from planned upgrades. For instance, work on APO (Any Prevout) in 2022 revealed the "Replacement Cycling Attack," affecting multiple potential use cases for APO. Addressing such vulnerabilities sometimes requires a dedicated soft-fork, as was publicly debated after disclosure. These technical hurdles can delay or deprioritize feature-focused upgrades, reaffirming the principle that security must take precedence over rapid protocol evolution. Community involvement remains critical to the progression of proposals like BIP54.
